title: Unit 4: Linear Momentum

guide.title: Linear momentum: review guide
guide.intro: Momentum is the quantity that forces change over time. Because internal forces come in equal and opposite pairs, a system's total momentum stays the same unless an outside force acts, which makes collisions solvable.
guide.equationNote: Momentum is a vector: in two dimensions, conserve the x- and y-components separately.

sections.title: Impulse and momentum
body: Momentum is p = mv. The impulse of a force is J = ∫F dt, the area under the F–t graph, and it equals the change in momentum: J = Δp.
Newton's second law in its general form is F_net = dp/dt. A longer collision time spreads the same momentum change over more time and lowers the average force.
points: A rebound reverses the momentum, so it needs a larger impulse than simply stopping.
Impulse is measured in N·s, the same unit as kg·m/s.

sections.title: Conservation of momentum
body: If the net external force on a system is zero, or negligible during a brief collision, its total momentum is conserved: Σmv before = Σmv after.
The center of mass of an isolated system moves at a constant velocity, v_cm = Σp/Σm, whatever happens inside it.
points: Recoil: objects that start at rest and push apart have equal and opposite momenta.
In two dimensions, write separate equations for x and y.
Momentum is conserved in every collision, elastic or not.

sections.title: Collisions and kinetic energy
body: In an elastic collision kinetic energy is also conserved. In an inelastic collision some kinetic energy becomes thermal energy or deformation; in a perfectly inelastic collision the objects stick together and lose as much kinetic energy as momentum conservation allows.
For a head-on elastic collision with the second object initially at rest: v₁′ = (m₁ − m₂)v₁/(m₁ + m₂) and v₂′ = 2m₁v₁/(m₁ + m₂).
points: Equal masses in a head-on elastic collision exchange velocities.
Check an answer by comparing the kinetic energy before and after.
Kinetic energy cannot increase in a collision unless stored energy is released, as in an explosion.

example.prompt: A 0.050 kg bullet moving at 400 m/s embeds itself in a 1.95 kg block at rest on a frictionless surface. Find their speed afterward and the kinetic energy lost.
example.solution: Momentum: (0.050)(400) = (2.0)v, so v = 10 m/s. K before = ½(0.050)(400)² = 4000 J; K after = ½(2.0)(10)² = 100 J. So 3900 J becomes thermal energy and deformation.

misconceptions: “Momentum is conserved only in elastic collisions.”
Momentum is conserved in every collision of an isolated system; kinetic energy is what may not be.
“A bigger force always means a bigger impulse.”
Impulse depends on both the force and how long it acts.
“A ball that bounces needs less force than one that stops.”
Bouncing changes the momentum more, so it needs a larger impulse.
“In 2D, add momentum magnitudes like plain numbers.”
Momentum is a vector; conserve each component separately.

questions.prompt: What is the momentum of a 0.15 kg baseball moving at 40 m/s?
choiceExplanations: 120 is ½mv² = 120 J, the kinetic energy, not the momentum.
267 is v/m; momentum is mass times velocity.
40.15 adds the mass and the speed.

questions.prompt: A 5.0 kg object at rest is pushed by a force F(t) = 10t newtons for 3.0 s. What is its speed at the end? (Ignore friction.)
questions.explanation: Impulse J = ∫₀³ 10t dt = 5t² from 0 to 3 = 45 N·s. Starting from rest, v = J/m = 45 ÷ 5.0 = 9.0 m/s.
choiceExplanations: 18 m/s treats the final force, 30 N, as if it acted for the whole 3.0 s.
6.0 is F(3)/m = 30/5.0, an acceleration at t = 3 s, not a speed.
45 is the impulse in N·s; divide by the mass to get the speed.

questions.prompt: A 0.20 kg ball hits a wall at 10 m/s and bounces straight back at 8.0 m/s. The contact lasts 0.020 s. What is the average force of the wall on the ball?
questions.explanation: Taking the rebound direction as positive, Δp = 0.20(8.0) − 0.20(−10) = 3.6 kg·m/s. Average force = Δp/Δt = 3.6 ÷ 0.020 = 180 N.
choiceExplanations: 20 N uses the change in speed, 10 − 8 = 2 m/s; the direction reverses, so the velocity changes by 18 m/s.
3.6 is the impulse in N·s; divide it by the contact time.
0.072 multiplies the impulse by the time instead of dividing.

questions.prompt: A 2.0 kg cart moving at 3.0 m/s collides with and sticks to a 1.0 kg cart at rest. How fast do they move together afterward?
questions.explanation: Momentum is conserved: (2.0)(3.0) = (3.0)v, so v = 2.0 m/s.
choiceExplanations: 3.0 m/s ignores the mass of the second cart, which must now move too.
1.5 m/s averages the speeds; momentum, not speed, is conserved.
6.0 is the total momentum in kg·m/s.

questions.prompt: A 60 kg skater at rest on frictionless ice throws a 2.0 kg ball forward at 15 m/s. What is the skater's velocity afterward?
questions.explanation: The total momentum stays zero: (2.0)(15) + (60)v = 0, so v = −0.50 m/s, which is 0.50 m/s opposite to the throw.
choiceExplanations: The skater and ball have equal and opposite momenta, not equal speeds; the skater is 30 times heavier.
To keep the total momentum zero, the skater must move opposite to the ball.
2.0 m/s divides the ball's momentum, 30 kg·m/s, by 15 instead of by the skater's mass.

questions.prompt: A 1.0 kg puck moving east at 5.0 m/s strikes an identical puck at rest on frictionless ice. Afterward, the first puck moves at 3.0 m/s, 53° north of east (cos 53° = 0.60, sin 53° = 0.80). What is the second puck's velocity?
questions.explanation: Conserve each component. East: 5.0 = 3.0(0.60) + v_x, so v_x = 3.2 m/s. North: 0 = 3.0(0.80) + v_y, so v_y = −2.4 m/s. Speed √(3.2² + 2.4²) = 4.0 m/s, at tan⁻¹(2.4/3.2) ≈ 37° south of east.
choiceExplanations: 2.0 m/s subtracts the speeds as plain numbers; momentum is a vector, so conserve each component.
The north components must cancel: the first puck gained north momentum, so the second must move south.
3.2 m/s is only the east component; the 2.4 m/s south component is missing.

questions.prompt: Two carts collide on a frictionless track and stick together. Which quantities are conserved in the collision?
choices: Total momentum, but not total kinetic energy
Total kinetic energy, but not total momentum
Both total momentum and total kinetic energy
questions.explanation: With no external horizontal force, momentum is conserved in every collision. When objects stick together (a perfectly inelastic collision), some kinetic energy becomes thermal energy and deformation.
choiceExplanations: It is the other way around: momentum is always conserved here, and kinetic energy is lost when objects stick.
Kinetic energy is conserved only in elastic collisions; sticking together is perfectly inelastic.
Momentum is conserved because no net external force acts on the two carts.

questions.prompt: A 2.0 kg cart moving at 3.0 m/s collides with and sticks to a 1.0 kg cart that was at rest. How much kinetic energy is lost?
questions.explanation: Before: ½(2.0)(3.0)² = 9.0 J. The carts move off together at (2.0 × 3.0)/3.0 = 2.0 m/s, so after: ½(3.0)(2.0)² = 6.0 J. The loss is 3.0 J.
choiceExplanations: 9.0 J is all of the starting kinetic energy; the carts keep moving, so some remains.
Kinetic energy is lost when objects stick together.
6.0 J is the kinetic energy left after the collision, not the amount lost.

questions.prompt: A 1.0 kg ball moving at 6.0 m/s makes a head-on elastic collision with a 2.0 kg ball at rest. What are their velocities afterward?
choices: 1.0 kg ball: −2.0 m/s; 2.0 kg ball: +4.0 m/s
questions.explanation: v₁′ = (1 − 2)(6.0)/3 = −2.0 m/s and v₂′ = 2(1)(6.0)/3 = +4.0 m/s. Check: momentum 6 = −2 + 8, and kinetic energy 18 J = 2 J + 16 J.
choiceExplanations: Moving together is a perfectly inelastic collision; an elastic collision conserves kinetic energy, and this would lose 12 J.
This conserves momentum but keeps only 9 J of the 18 J of kinetic energy, so it is not elastic.
This gives 12 kg·m/s of momentum from 6 kg·m/s; the velocities are exchanged only when the masses are equal.
